lesson.subtitle: Lesson 20 -- Midpoint Milestone
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Aguinaldo Ballon | Lesson 20 -- Midpoint Milestone

listenings.text: I have organized more than two hundred panels, and I can tell you a secret. The best panelists are not the ones with the best English. They are the ones with a clear point of view. Before every forum, I call each panelist and ask one question: what do you want the audience to remember? If they can answer in one sentence, the panel will work. If they cannot, it does not matter how fluent they are. My other advice is simple. Do not read your opening remarks. Look at the audience, speak slowly, and finish on time. Nobody ever complained that a panelist was too short.

The first time a conference in London invited me, I said no. I told them I was too busy, but the truth was different. I was afraid that somebody would ask a question I could not understand. Two years later, they invited me again. This time I said yes, and I prepared for six weeks. I rehearsed my opening remarks every morning, and I asked a colleague to play the moderator. On the day, I was nervous for the first two minutes. After that, I forgot about my English and talked about my work. A partner from a fund came to me after the panel, and that conversation became my biggest client.

defs: to say no to an offer or an invitation
an important idea you plan to mention

being calm and in control under pressure
the fear you feel before you speak in public
to practice a speech before the real event

paras: Every year, conference organizers send thousands of invitations to experts, and a surprising number of them say no. The reasons are rarely about time. Many experienced professionals turn down a panel because they are afraid of one moment: a question they cannot answer, in a language that is not their first. Interestingly, the people who say no are often the people the audience most wants to hear.

Moderators say the fear comes from a wrong idea of what a panel is. A panel is not an exam. Nobody expects a panelist to give a perfect speech. The audience wants three things: a clear point of view, real examples, and honesty. A speaker with simple English who gets his point across is more useful than a speaker with perfect grammar and nothing to say. Stage fright is normal, even for professionals who speak every week. What the audience notices is not the fear, but the composure.

Experienced panelists prepare in a simple way. First, they choose three talking points and connect each one to a real case. Second, they rehearse their opening remarks out loud until they can say them without notes. Third, they prepare a short answer for the question they fear most. As soon as the panel starts, they stop thinking about grammar and start thinking about the audience. The best moments are often off the cuff, but they come from good preparation. For many professionals, saying yes to the first panel is a milestone. It is rarely the last.
